extraction_meta.note: Two further observations were discarded under the fabrication guard: a general claim about 'multilingual models being harder to fine-tune' and one about 'benchmarks needing real data'. Both are true and both are generic — neither traced to anything specific that happened this session.

candidates.title: Language-specific ASR models can score worse than general ones on code-switched speech
candidates.body:
IndicWhisper outperforms Whisper large-v3 on monolingual Hindi by a clear margin, and that is what its published benchmarks measure. On intra-sentential code-switching — a Hindi sentence containing English technical terms — it degrades sharply, because the fine-tuning that specialised it toward Hindi also narrowed its English handling.

The general lesson: a model specialised for language X may be worse than a general model when the real input is X mixed with Y. Published benchmarks rarely measure the mixed case, so the specialised model looks strictly better on paper and is not.

Check what the benchmark actually measured before trusting a comparison.
candidates.basis: Benchmarked both models on 40 minutes of real recorded lecture audio. Results recorded in Projects/classmind/.knowledge/benchmarks/asr-comparison.md. IndicWhisper won on the monolingual segments and lost on every code-switched segment.

candidates.title: Use Whisper large-v3 as the ASR baseline for ClassMind
candidates.body:
Decision: Whisper large-v3, not IndicWhisper.

Reason: code-switched audio is the dominant case in our recordings, and large-v3 handles it materially better.

Alternatives: IndicWhisper (better on pure Hindi, worse on the case we actually have); commercial APIs (better accuracy, per-minute cost incompatible with a student-facing free tier).

Trade-offs: large-v3 is slower and needs more VRAM, which constrains our deployment target and may force batch rather than near-real-time processing. Accepted for now; revisit if latency becomes a product requirement.
candidates.basis: Explicit decision taken during this session and already written into Projects/classmind/.knowledge/decisions.md.

candidates.title: Does the code-switching penalty hold across speakers, or is it an artefact of our sample?
candidates.body:
The 40-minute benchmark came from three lecturers in one department. Code-switching density varies a lot by individual, subject and institution. If our sample happens to be unusually dense, the measured gap may not generalise — and the model choice rests on it.

Resolving this needs audio from a wider set of lecturers before the decision in cand-002 can be treated as settled rather than provisional.
candidates.basis: Raised explicitly during the session while reviewing the benchmark's composition; not resolved before the session ended.
